titre: The Tale of Genji, the World's First Novel
accroche: Murasaki Shikibu's father regretted that she was not born a boy: she understood classical Chinese better than her brother.
contenu_vulgarise:
In her diary, Murasaki Shikibu recounts a scene from her childhood, in her father's house in Kyoto, around the year 980. Her brother is learning classical Chinese, the learned language reserved for men; she listens to the lesson beside him, and picks up the hardest passages faster than he does. Her father, a respected scholar, is dismayed: “Just my luck!” he would say. “What a pity she was not born a man!”

## A Closed Language, a Language Left to Women

At the Heian court, two scripts coexist, and they are not socially equal. Classical Chinese (*kanbun*) is used for government, administration, everything that counts officially, and its study is reserved for men. *Kana*, a phonetic alphabet invented to transcribe spoken Japanese, is considered a minor genre, barely good enough for intimate letters, poems, and the diaries of court women. It is even called *onnade*, “women's hand.”

Murasaki, who has secretly mastered Chinese, nonetheless chooses to write in kana. It is not a lack of talent: it is the only script socially open to her. Between 1000 and 1012 or so, she composes in it *Genji Monogatari* (*The Tale of Genji*), fifty-four chapters that follow the romantic and political life of Prince Genji over several decades, with constant attention to what his characters feel, not only to what happens to them. It is precisely this criterion, psychological depth sustained over the long haul, that leads many scholars to speak, for this work, of the world's first novel rather than of a mere fictional chronicle.

## What This Shifts

In the West, the novel is readily said to begin with Cervantes's *Don Quixote*, in 1605, often called the first modern novel. The formula is not false: Cervantes invents an ironic distance between narrator and character that, in Europe, is found nowhere before him. But it implies, without saying so, that the novel begins in Europe. *The Tale of Genji* precedes *Don Quixote* by nearly six hundred years, written by a woman to whom learned writing was closed, in a language judged too minor to count.

The irony is complete: it is precisely because kana did not count, in the eyes of the court, that it became the space where a literary form that the whole world still uses today was invented, without anyone seeking it.

citation.texte: When my brother [...] was a young boy learning the Chinese classics, I was in the habit of listening with him and I became unusually proficient at understanding those passages that he found too difficult to grasp and memorize. Father, a most learned man, was always regretting the fact: 'Just my luck!' he would say. 'What a pity she was not born a man!'
citation.source: Murasaki Shikibu Nikki (Diary of Murasaki Shikibu), c. 1010, trans. Richard Bowring

carte.punch: Her father regretted that she was a girl. According to many, she wrote the world's first novel.
carte.idee: The Tale of Genji, composed between 1000 and 1012 or so by Murasaki Shikibu, is considered by many scholars to be the world's first novel, nearly six hundred years before Don Quixote, often called the first modern novel.

quiz.question: Why does Murasaki Shikibu write The Tale of Genji in kana rather than in classical Chinese, which she had nonetheless mastered?
choix: Because classical Chinese had disappeared from the Japanese imperial court in the 11th century
Because she did not know classical Chinese well enough to write a long text
Because Chinese, reserved for learned men, was closed to her, and only kana, judged minor, remained open to women
Because the emperor had explicitly commissioned a work written in the language of the people
quiz.explication: Murasaki mastered Chinese better than her brother, to her father's regret, so it is not a question of competence. But classical Chinese remained the official language reserved for men; kana, judged minor, was the only writing space open to court women. It is in this space judged secondary that the novel is invented, without anyone seeking it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the name of the Japanese phonetic alphabet in which Murasaki Shikibu wrote her work?
choix: Kanbun, the learned language reserved for administration
Manyogana, an ancient Buddhist transcription system
Rōmaji, the Latin transcription of Japanese
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kana, a phonetic alphabet invented to transcribe spoken Japanese, is nicknamed onnade, “women's hand,” and was regarded as a minor kind of writing.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many chapters does The Tale of Genji have, and over what span of time does it unfold?
choix: Fifty-four chapters, following Prince Genji's life over several decades
Twelve chapters, centered on a single year at the imperial court
One hundred eight chapters, divided into twelve separate volumes
Thirty-six chapters, each devoted to a different character
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The work has fifty-four chapters that follow the romantic and political life of Prince Genji over several decades, with constant attention to what his characters feel.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What criterion leads many scholars to call The Tale of Genji the world's first novel?
choix: The exceptional number of named secondary characters in the plot
The psychological depth of the characters sustained over the whole length of the work
The exclusive use of kana, never before used in a long text
The presence of an outside narrator distinct from the author herself
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is the constant attention paid to what the characters feel, sustained over the long haul, that leads scholars to speak of a first novel rather than a mere chronicle.
